video.title: Attention and transformers: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, explained
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Dr Salma - statistics lecturer, Cairo University (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: Take the sentence: the student couldn't fit the laptop in the bag because it was full. What does it refer to? People answer instantly. Older language models often guessed the laptop.
Today: scaled dot-product attention, why it is divided by the square root of d, and how to teach the transformer without drowning students.
Attention lets every token build its new representation as a weighted average of all the tokens. The weights say how relevant each other token is. So it can look straight at the bag.
Each token makes three vectors. Its query asks what it needs, each key says what a token offers, and values carry the content. Scores are queries times keys, divided by root d, then softmax.
Here are one head's attention weights from it to the other nouns. Most of the weight goes to bag. The student and the laptop get little.

If query and key entries have mean zero and variance one, their dot product has variance d. Large scores push softmax into saturation, where gradients vanish. Dividing by root d keeps the variance near one.

Vaswani and colleagues' diagram has too much in it for a first lecture. Start with one head, three tokens and two dimensions. Students compute the scores by hand, then you add heads, layers and positions.
Quick check! The key dimension d is sixty four. By what number do we divide the raw attention scores?
Eight, the square root of sixty four. Without it, scores would have a standard deviation near eight and softmax would almost always pick one token.
In the app, open the attention lab. Tap the word “it” and see which words it attends to. Switch the ending from “hungry” to “fresh”, and watch its attention move from “dog” to “milk”.
Your turn. Attention alone treats its inputs as a set. What does the transformer add so word order matters?
Positional encodings. Remember: attention is a weighted average, scores are queries times keys over root d, and position must be added.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lecture
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lecture: give pairs two-dimensional query, key and value vectors for three tokens. They compute the scores, the softmax and the output by hand, then compare with three lines of NumPy.

checkpoints.prompt: The key dimension d is 64. By what do we divide the raw attention scores?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: √64 = 8, which keeps the scores' variance near 1.

checkpoints.prompt: Attention alone treats inputs as a set. What makes word order matter?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: position information is added to each token's embedding.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: without positional encodings, shuffling the words gives the same outputs, just reordered.
